title: Rift Valley Fever
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Rift Valley fever is a mosquito‑borne Phenuiviridae infection causing a spectrum from mild febrile illness to severe hepatitis, hemorrhage, and encephalitis. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, serology or PCR, and supportive care is the mainstay of treatment.

sections.p: Rift Valley fever (RVF) is an arboviral disease endemic to sub‑Saharan Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. Outbreaks follow heavy rains that boost mosquito populations. In low‑resource hospitals, patients often present with fever, headache, and nonspecific malaise before complications develop.
b: Case fatality up to 10 % in severe forms
Occupational risk: herders, abattoir workers, veterinarians

sections.p: RVFV is a single‑stranded, negative‑sense RNA virus in the family Phenuiviridae. It replicates in the cytoplasm of infected cells and can infect a wide range of mammals.
b: Stable in dried blood for weeks

sections.p: The virus circulates between livestock (sheep, goats, cattle) and mosquitoes. Humans acquire infection via bite of infected Aedes or Culex mosquitoes, or through contact with blood/tissues of viremic animals.
b: Vertical transmission in Aedes eggs (explains sudden outbreaks)
Mechanical transmission by other biting insects is possible

sections.p: RVF presents in three clinical patterns: a mild flu‑like syndrome, a severe hepatic‑hemorrhagic form, and a neuroinvasive form. Severity is influenced by age, pregnancy, and underlying liver disease.
b: Mild: fever, myalgia, arthralgia, retro‑orbital pain
Severe: jaundice, elevated transaminases, hemorrhagic diathesis, renal failure
Neuro: meningitis, encephalitis, seizures, focal deficits

sections.p: In resource‑limited settings, clinical suspicion guides early management. Confirmatory tests are serology (IgM ELISA) and RT‑PCR; both may be unavailable, requiring reliance on epidemiology and basic labs.

t.b: Is there thrombocytopenia or leukopenia? Low platelets support hemorrhagic risk; normal counts do not exclude disease
Are transaminases markedly raised? Values >5 × ULN suggest severe hepatic involvement

t.a: IgM ELISA for RVFV (if lab exists)
t.b: Positive IgM indicates recent infection; negative early in disease does not rule out infection

t.a: RT‑PCR on serum or whole blood
t.b: Detects viral RNA within first 5 days; a positive result confirms diagnosis

t.a: If serology/PCR unavailable, use WHO case definition
t.b: Fever + epidemiologic link + any two: jaundice, hemorrhage, encephalitis → probable case

sections.p: No specific antiviral is approved. Management is supportive, focusing on organ protection, hemorrhage control, and prevention of secondary infections.
b: Transfusion of platelets or fresh frozen plasma for active bleeding
Empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics only if bacterial superinfection suspected
Ribavirin may be used experimentally where available, but toxicity limits routine use

t.b: Detect early renal failure; initiate renal protective measures
Guide intensity of hepatic support and need for transfer to higher‑level care

sections.p: Examiners love to test integration of epidemiology, pattern recognition, and pragmatic management in low‑resource settings.
b: Always ask about recent floods, livestock exposure, or animal abortions
Distinguish RVF from malaria (fever + hepatomegaly) by presence of hemorrhage or encephalitis
Remember that a normal platelet count does not exclude early RVF

faq.q: Can RVF be prevented by vaccination?
faq.a: A veterinary live‑attenuated vaccine exists for animals; no licensed human vaccine is currently available.

faq.q: Is ribavirin recommended for routine treatment?
faq.a: Ribavirin is not standard; it is reserved for severe cases in research settings because of hemolytic anemia risk.

faq.q: How long does IgM remain positive?
faq.a: IgM can persist for 3–6 months, so a positive result indicates recent but not necessarily acute infection.

exam: A 28‑year‑old shepherd presents with fever, jaundice, and a recent outbreak of livestock abortions – what is your next diagnostic step? — Use the WHO case definition and order IgM ELISA or PCR if available; otherwise manage as probable RVF.
How does RVF differ from severe malaria in a patient with fever and hepatomegaly? — Highlight hemorrhagic signs, lack of parasitemia, and epidemiologic link to mosquitoes or animal exposure.

A patient with RVF develops a platelet count of 45 × 10⁹/L and active epistaxis – what is the immediate management? — Give platelet transfusion and consider fresh frozen plasma; monitor for further bleeding.
Why is ribavirin not first‑line therapy for RVF despite in‑vitro activity? — Toxicity (hemolytic anemia), limited clinical data, and need for supportive care outweigh benefits.
In a setting without PCR, which combination of clinical and basic lab findings makes RVF most likely? — Fever, recent flood exposure, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, and transaminases >5 × ULN.

What are the key infection‑control measures for health‑care workers caring for RVF patients? — Use standard precautions, wear gloves and eye protection when handling blood or animal tissues; no airborne precautions needed.
A pregnant woman contracts RVF – what specific risk does she face? — High risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, and severe maternal hemorrhage.

How would you differentiate RVF encephalitis from viral meningitis in a low‑resource ward? — Look for focal neurologic deficits, seizures, and a recent outbreak; CSF may show lymphocytic pleocytosis but is not definitive.
